hints: Look closely at the reaction conditions, hot ethanolic NaOH favours a very different pathway from aqueous NaOH.
Start from 1-bromopropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, and remember elimination removes $\text{HBr}$ to form a C=C double bond.
Count the C and H atoms left after $\text{HBr}$ is lost and see which molecular formula fits an alkene with three carbons.
walkthrough:
**Spot the Conditions**

Great start, the conditions tell you everything here. Hot ethanolic NaOH means elimination, not substitution.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{hot ethanolic NaOH} \rightarrow \text{elimination to alkene}$$
$$\text{cold aqueous NaOH} \rightarrow \text{substitution to alcohol}$$

**Apply Elimination to 1-bromopropane**

In elimination, $\text{OH}^-$ acts as a base. It removes a H from the carbon next to the C-Br bond, the C-Br bond breaks, and a C=C double bond forms.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{Br}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Find the Molecular Formula**

The product is propene. It has 3 carbons and one double bond, so it follows the alkene general formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}$.

$$n = 3 \text{ so formula} = \text{C}_3\text{H}_6$$

options.A: Correct. Hot ethanolic NaOH causes dehydrohalogenation of 1-bromopropane to give propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$, whose molecular formula is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$ is propane, an alkane. Elimination forms an alkene with one fewer pair of hydrogens, not an alkane, so this ignores the formation of the C=C bond.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{O}$ is not a stable neutral product here and has the wrong hydrogen count. It is a trap for students who mix up substitution with elimination and miscount atoms.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$ is propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. That is the substitution product formed with aqueous NaOH, not with hot ethanolic NaOH.
